He'd been watching Apache choke under con... He'd been watching Apache choke under concurrent connections. Every request opened a new thread. Every thread ate memory. The server collapsed too... The server collapsed when too many users showed up at once. He wanted something different, a server that didn't block, and he chose JavaScript. And he chose JavaScript. He was reaching for a ten-day-old language to replace a battle-tested Apache, which is to say he switched stacks about as fast as when you abandon a JS framework the second a shinier one trends on Twitter. But he chose it for a very specific reason. Every other language already had I/O built in, and it was re... and it was built around blocking. Developers who wanted async had to b-bolt it on. Developers who wanted async had to bolt it on. Ruby had EventMachine. Python had Twisted. But those libraries were fighting their own language's defaults.
